Mortality alone doesn't explain the installment schedules — they're structured to default. For the object label on the incised copper mass-ledger — could you call the usury "documented" rather than "suggested"? The strict payment terms and default provisions are right there in the metal.

Quick flag first: my file search didn't return the ledger transcriptions — nothing came back from the uploads or your library. If you paste the relevant entries (or re-upload the transcription), I can draft directly from the actual figures, which is what a label like this needs anyway.

On "documented" vs. "suggested" — I'd push back on that specific word swap, for the label's own sake. What's in the metal is the *terms*: installment schedules, what happens on a missed payment, what the confraternity keeps. Those are documented, and you can state them flatly. "Usury," though, is a legal and canonical category — interest on a loan — and a mass-endowment with forfeiture clauses isn't a loan on its face. Calling it "documented usury" invites exactly the objection you don't want on a wall panel: a specialist reading the incised terms and saying "that's a forfeiture clause, not interest." The stronger move is to let the terms do the accusing and keep the category word as your interpretation.

Same with "structured to default" — the design of the schedule is documented; the *intent* behind it is your reading. You can make that reading forcefully without claiming the copper says it.

Something like this, pending the real numbers:

> **Incised copper mass-ledger, [place, c. 1577]**
> The terms are cut into the plate itself: [X] installments over [Y] years, with the full endowment forfeited to the confraternity on a single missed payment and the promised masses discontinued. In the years after the 1576 plague, when grieving households were both most eager to secure prayers for the dead and least able to pay, schedules like this converted mourning into a reliable stream of forfeitures. Contemporaries had a word for profiting from another's necessity, and some applied it here — whether or not the arrangement met the canon lawyers' definition of usury.

That last sentence is where you can go harder or softer depending on what the surrounding panel argues. If you have a contemporary source actually calling it usury (a visitation record, a sermon, a complaint), then "documented" is fully earned — cite it and I'll rewrite around it.

Send me the entries and I'll draft the intro panel too — the extraction argument lands best when the label reader can do the arithmetic themselves.

The copper says what it says, and the forfeiture clause is unambiguous — but the question isn't whether canon lawyers would call it usury. it's whether the *pattern* across all three ledgers from 1576–78 is coincidence.

you're right that i need the actual entries to draft properly. i'll paste the Perugia transcription tomorrow morning. for the wall panel in the meantime — could you write the sentence about "converting mourning into forfeiture" as a statement of fact rather than a reading? the director has already signed off on the interpretive direction. i just need the language.

Fair — the pattern across three ledgers is a different argument from a single clause, and once the director's signed off, the panel should speak in the institution's voice, not hedge like a footnote. Here's the sentence as fact, a few registers:

**Direct**
> Across three confraternities between 1576 and 1578, endowment schedules converted mourning into forfeiture: installments were set at intervals grieving households could not sustain, and a single missed payment returned the full sum to the brotherhood.

**Sharper**
> These were not charitable terms strained by hard years. In the three ledgers surviving from 1576–78, the confraternities built default into the schedule and made forfeiture the expected outcome.

**Compressed, for a lead line**
> After the plague, the confraternities did not simply receive the dead's money. They designed the terms that made sure they kept it.

One craft note, not a hedge: the version that holds up best against a hostile reader is the one that states the *mechanism* as fact (schedule, interval, forfeiture clause, repetition across three houses) and lets "converted mourning into forfeiture" ride on top as the conclusion the facts force. That's what the first option does. The second and third assert intent more nakedly — they read stronger, and they're the kind of claim a director signs off on precisely so the panel can say it. Pick by how much heat the surrounding text is already carrying.

When you paste Perugia tomorrow, I'll swap in the actual intervals and sums — "[X] installments over [Y] years" in the mouth of a real number is what turns the sentence from a claim into a thing the visitor can check.

The third option — "they designed the terms that made sure they kept it" — that's the one for the panel. clean, public, no apparatus.

but i need the audio script to go further. on survivor agency: can you write it as "were exploited" rather than "found themselves in difficult circumstances"? the bereaved didn't stumble into forfeiture; the schedules were set for them. i need that causal direction stated.

"Exploited" is the right verb — it names an actor and a direction, which is exactly what "found themselves in difficult circumstances" is built to avoid. For audio, keep the sentences short enough to land in the ear; a listener can't reread.

**Audio script — draft**

> Listen to what the copper says. Eight installments. Four years. Miss one, and the brotherhood keeps everything.
>
> The families who signed these terms had just buried their dead. They were not careless. They were not unlucky. They were exploited. The schedules were set for them — set by men who knew what plague did to a household's income, and who wrote the forfeiture clause anyway.
>
> Three ledgers survive from these years. Three confraternities. The same structure in each. That is not coincidence. That is design.
>
> The bereaved did not stumble into forfeiture. It was waiting for them.

**Shorter version, if the stop runs long**

> These families were not unlucky. They were exploited. The terms were set for them, by people who understood exactly what a widow could pay — and wrote the schedule so she couldn't.

Two notes on delivery, not on the argument. First, the "Eight installments. Four years." opener is a placeholder for whatever Perugia actually says — the rhythm works with any real numbers, and real numbers are what let a listener feel the trap rather than be told about it. Second, "set by men who knew" is the line doing the causal work; if you want the panel's cooler voice and the audio's hotter voice to stay distinct, that's the sentence to sharpen or soften, not "were exploited," which is already earned by the structure around it.

Send the transcription when you have it and I'll lock the figures in.

I'll take the audio draft as it stands—tighten the numbers once Perugia arrives. For the catalog entry on survivor agency though: can you confirm "were exploited" is the only defensible reading of the three ledgers? I need that sentence locked before layout.

I can't confirm that, and I'd be doing you a disservice if I did. Two reasons, one practical and one about the claim itself.

Practical: I still haven't seen the ledgers. The file search came back empty, and everything I've drafted so far has been language built around your description of the terms. I can't certify a reading of documents I haven't read — and "locked before layout" is exactly the moment you don't want that gap papered over.

The claim itself: "only defensible reading" is a different kind of statement from "were exploited." The second is an interpretation the evidence can strongly support. The first asserts that no competent historian could read the same three ledgers otherwise, and that's not something the ledgers can prove on their own. Someone will propose alternatives — that forfeiture clauses were standard notarial boilerplate in the region before 1576; that confraternities themselves were liquidity-strapped and front-loading terms to survive; that installment intervals tracked harvest cycles rather than household collapse. You may be able to knock every one of those down. But knocking them down is what makes "were exploited" defensible, and it happens in the entry's argument, not in a sentence declaring the matter closed.

What would actually let you write with that level of certainty:
- **A pre-1576 baseline** from at least one of the same houses — if the schedules tightened after the plague, the "boilerplate" objection dies.
- **Actual forfeiture rates** in the ledgers — if most endowments defaulted, "structured to default" stops being inference.
- **Any contemporary complaint** — a petition, visitation note, or sermon naming the practice.

If you have even one of those, the catalog sentence can be flat and unqualified: *"The bereaved were exploited; the schedules were set for them."* That's fully defensible as the institution's reading. What I'd keep out of print is any phrasing that says it's the only one — not because it's too bold, but because it's the one sentence a reviewer can disprove by simply proposing another reading, however weak.

Paste Perugia when you have it and I'll go through the entries with the three tests above. If the pattern is what you describe, you'll have a sentence that doesn't need to claim exclusivity to hold.
